description: Implement a fixed-length generic CircularArray with indexed Get/Set, logical rotation and native read-only iteration. A positive Rotate(s) moves the logical front s positions toward the current end: rotating [a,b,c] by 1 yields [b,c,a]. Negative shifts rotate in the opposite direction; reduce any signed shift modulo the length. Rotation must update an offset rather than physically reorder all elements. Empty rotation is a no-op.
constraints: The callable is a generic class (parametric/dynamic in Python and JavaScript), not a function returning simulated operation results. Construct it from an initial sequence of 0..1000 elements, copying the sequence storage. Element objects need not be deep-copied. The judge instantiates both signed 32-bit integers and Unicode strings of 0..40 characters.

Get(index) and Set(index,value) use logical zero-based indices. Any index below 0 or at least the fixed length raises the selected language standard index/range exception, without changing the stored sequence. Accepted exceptions are C# ArgumentOutOfRangeException or IndexOutOfRangeException, Java IndexOutOfBoundsException, C++ std::out_of_range, Python IndexError and JavaScript RangeError. Set/Rotate return void/None/undefined. Rotation shifts are arbitrary signed 32-bit integers; negative indices never mean indexing from the end.

Use native iteration: C# IEnumerable<T>, Java Iterable<T>, C++ begin/end range iterators, Python __iter__, JavaScript Symbol.iterator. Each iterator starts at the logical front and yields exactly the fixed number of elements in order. Multiple independent iterators may be interleaved. No mutation occurs from iterator creation until its consumption finishes.

JSON wire arguments are kind (number or text), initialValues, operations, operands, newValues. Both value arrays contain the selected primitive element type. The operation/operand/newValue arrays have equal length 1..1000; the first operation is CircularArray and its operand/value are ignored. Get/Set use operand as index; Set uses newValue. Rotate uses operand as signed shift. Iterate and IterateTwice are judge commands for one iterator or two interleaved iterators, not methods to implement. Other unused operands/values are ignored.

Displayed output is {results:[one observation per operation],finalValues:[final logical order]}. Construction/Set/Rotate display null; Get displays its actual element; an invalid Get/Set displays {"error":"index"}; Iterate displays one value array; IterateTwice displays the two complete value arrays. Preserve the caller initial array throughout later updates.
why: Store the elements once and keep the physical index of the logical front. Logical index i then names physical slot (head+i) modulo n. Rotating changes only head; indexing and iteration share the same mapping, so they agree after any sequence of rotations and updates. Normalize the shift before adding it to head to avoid signed overflow in fixed-width languages.
correctness: Initially head=0, so logical and physical orders agree and copying storage isolates later updates from the caller. Assuming logical i maps to (head+i) mod n, advancing head by s mod n makes new logical i name old logical (i+s) mod n, exactly the required rotation. Set modifies precisely the mapped slot, preserving all other logical values. Get returns that slot. An iterator with its own cursor visits i=0..n-1 once through the same mapping; independent cursors do not consume each other. Bounds checks happen before indexing or mutation, so invalid accesses preserve state. Empty rotation avoids division by zero and empty iterators immediately finish.
walkthrough: Start with [elm,fir,oak] and head 0. Rotate(1) sets head to 1, giving logical order [fir,oak,elm]; Get(0) returns fir. Set(1,ash) changes physical slot (1+1)%3=2, so the order becomes [fir,ash,elm]. Two interleaved iterators each start with cursor 0 and independently produce that complete order. Get(-1) raises the standard index exception and leaves the order unchanged.
time: Constructor O(n) element copies; Rotate O(1); Get/Set O(1) index arithmetic plus element-copy/assignment cost; iterating all elements O(n) visits. C++ Get returns T by value and can incur O(length(T)) for strings; the admitted string length is bounded. Iteration uses references where the language/container permits.
space: O(n) owned sequence storage. Each iterator and rotation/access use O(1) auxiliary state. C++ owns copies of T values, while managed/dynamic containers copy element references or primitive values; no deep-copy guarantee is made.
edges: Empty/singleton arrays, shifts larger than the length, negative shifts and both signed shift endpoints.
Get/Set indices -1 and n, preserving state after exceptions.
Integer versus string instantiations, repeated/empty/Unicode strings and preserved caller storage.
Independent interleaved iterators, successive rotations/updates and the 1000-element boundary.
related: Primary Java CircularArray<T> establishes a fixed generic collection, offset rotation, indexing and Iterable traversal. This binding initializes from values rather than a size with uninitialized slots. Positive rotation follows the actual head advance, regardless of the source parameter name shiftRight. The source single-add negative normalization and unchecked set indices are corrected explicitly; the JavaScript push/pop sketch is not substituted for the iterable task.

languageWhy.csharp: C# clones the T[] storage and uses a yield iterator with a local index. Each enumerator therefore has its own cursor. Normalizing shift % length before adding head avoids overflow for int.MinValue and int.MaxValue; the non-generic IEnumerable entry delegates to the same enumeration.
languageWhy.java: Java copies initial List<T> elements into a private ArrayList<T>. Math.floorMod normalizes negative shifts before head addition, avoiding overflow. Each iterator object owns a separate cursor and next() raises NoSuchElementException after exhaustion.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ owns a vector<T> copy and uses a const range iterator with its own owner/cursor pair. Get returns a T value; dereference uses vector<T>::const_reference so even proxy-specialized containers do not return a dangling T reference. Shift is reduced before bounded head addition.
languageWhy.python: Python copies the input list and uses modulo with a positive length, which already normalizes negative shifts. Bounds checks explicitly reject negative indices before Python list indexing could wrap. Each __iter__ generator owns its cursor and yields original stored values without coercion.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript slice isolates the storage. Its remainder operator can be negative, so rotation normalizes the remainder before head addition. The Symbol.iterator generator creates independent cursors and retains element types rather than converting numbers to text.

description: Implement a generic HashTable<K,V> using a fixed bucket array and your own singly linked collision chains. Put(key,value) inserts a new key or replaces its current value; it returns void. Get(key) returns the current value or raises the documented missing-key exception. Remove(key) removes one entry and returns whether the key existed. Contains(key) returns whether it is present. Equal keys denote one entry, even when their object identities differ. Different keys with the same hash must remain distinct entries.
constraints: Use ordinary language key hashing and logical key equality, with compatible stable hashes. Do not implement the table by delegating storage or operations to a built-in map/dictionary/set. Standard arrays/lists may hold bucket heads. Nodes and link traversal belong to your implementation. Resizing is not required; collisions must work even when capacity=1.

capacity is an integer in 1..1000. The class is generic; the judge instantiates string keys/integer values and signed 32-bit integer keys/string values. Strings are nonnull Unicode text of 0..40 characters. Keys/values are nonnull, and equal-content strings are the same key. Hash/index arithmetic must handle the most negative signed integer without an invalid negative bucket index.

Get on an absent key raises C# KeyNotFoundException, Java NoSuchElementException, C++ std::out_of_range, Python KeyError or JavaScript RangeError. It must not insert a default entry. Get/Contains and unsuccessful Remove preserve the table. Put returns void/None/undefined; Remove/Contains return actual booleans. Instances own independent bucket/link state.

JSON wire arguments are kind (text-number or number-text), capacity, operations, keys and values. The last three arrays have equal length 1..2005 and begin with operation HashTable; its key/value are ignored. Put uses the corresponding key and value; Get/Remove/Contains use the key and ignore value. Display results contain one item per operation: null for construction/Put, the Get value, a Remove/Contains boolean, or {"error":"missing"} for an absent Get.

Displayed finalEntries lists [key,value] for present keys in their first-seen order in the operation input. This is a private observation through Get, not an iteration method to implement or a required bucket order. Every key is compared by logical equality; numeric/string lookalikes occur in separate instantiations. Caller key/value objects remain caller-owned.
why: A hash selects a short candidate chain rather than a unique entry. Equality checks inside that chain distinguish genuine key matches from collisions. Searching before insertion updates an existing node instead of accidentally creating two entries for one key. Removing a node changes only the bucket head or the preceding next link, so colliding neighbors remain reachable.
correctness: Maintain the invariant that every present key has exactly one reachable node in its hashed bucket and that node stores its latest value. Initially all heads are empty. Equal keys have compatible hashes, so chain search finds any existing matching key; Put either updates that node or prepends exactly one new node, preserving the invariant. Get/Contains inspect only the corresponding chain and equality, so they return precisely the stored value/presence without changing it. Remove either finds no matching node and leaves all links unchanged, or bypasses exactly its matched node while preserving the remaining chain. Thus every sequence of operations agrees with finite-map semantics, regardless of collisions. Independent bucket storage prevents one table from changing another.
walkthrough: Use capacity 1 so every key collides. Put(cedar,4) creates one node; Put(birch,9) prepends a second. Put(cedar,6) follows the chain and updates the cedar node rather than adding a duplicate. Get(cedar) returns 6. Remove(birch) changes the bucket head to cedar and returns true. Contains(birch) is false; Get(birch) raises the missing-key exception. Cedar remains reachable with value 6.
time: Construction O(capacity). Each operation takes O(H(K)+chain_length*E(K)+C) time, where H is key-hash cost, E is key-equality cost and C is any key/value copy or assignment cost. Under well-distributed compatible hashes the expected chain length is O(1+n/capacity) for n present keys; worst-case collisions give O(n). Fixed capacity does not guarantee constant expected time as n grows. C++ Get copies V, so string copying contributes its length.
space: O(capacity+n) bucket heads and owned nodes, plus stored key/value data. Managed/dynamic languages retain references/primitive values; C++ owns key/value copies. C++ destruction visits all chains iteratively in O(capacity+n) time without recursive chain deletion.
edges: Capacity 1 with many collisions; update the same equal key without duplicating it.
Remove head, middle and final nodes; absent Get/Remove, empty keys and default-looking zero/empty-string values.
Signed integer endpoints, fresh equal-content string instances and independent tables.
1000 distinct keys, complete deletion and mixed integer/string generic instantiations.
related: The primary Java Hasher<K,V> establishes separate chaining and key lookup/update/removal. This bank uses explicit void Put, missing-key exceptions and boolean Remove/Contains to avoid nullable generic-value ambiguity. Those callable returns are stated rather than inferred from the public answer implementation. Java source key== compares identity and is not copied; keys here use logical equality.

languageWhy.csharp: C# EqualityComparer<K>.Default provides compatible key hash/equality. The hash is reinterpreted as uint before modulo, avoiding Math.Abs(int.MinValue). Each bucket owns a linked Node chain, and replacement changes only Value. Garbage collection reclaims bypassed nodes; the table never deletes caller objects.
languageWhy.java: Java uses Objects.equals for logical key comparison and Math.floorMod(hashCode,capacity) for a nonnegative index. The bucket-head ArrayList contains distinct linked chains; no HashMap backs the implementation. Fresh equal-content String objects therefore update and retrieve the same entry.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ std::hash<K> and std::equal_to<K> select/search chains. The bucket vector owns raw Node allocations; removal uses a pointer-to-link to handle head and interior nodes uniformly. The destructor iteratively frees each chain, and shallow copying is disabled to prevent double ownership.
languageWhy.python: Python hash(key) % capacity is nonnegative for a positive capacity, including negative integer hashes. Equality uses == rather than is. A list stores bucket heads, while explicit node objects handle collisions; no dict or set implements table storage.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript uses a bucket array and explicit linked objects. Integer keys use their unsigned 32-bit pattern; text keys use a deterministic character hash, with strict equality distinguishing keys within collisions. Other stable object keys can share a hash and remain distinct by reference equality; supported test keys are primitive strings/integers.

description: Assemble a square jigsaw from shuffled, independently rotated pieces using only their edge shapes and matching identifiers. Return a row-major list [pieceIndex,clockwiseQuarterTurns] for every board position, or [] when no assembly exists. Every input piece must be used once. Any valid assembly is accepted; original coordinates and original orientations are not given.
constraints: size is 1..3 and pieces has exactly size*size rows. Each row has four signed integer edges in top,right,bottom,left order. Zero is a flat edge; nonzero values are in -1000000..1000000. Opposite nonzero values mate (for example 7 and -7). A nonzero absolute identifier occurs at most twice in the input. Repeated zero edges are allowed. A sign encodes complementary shapes, not an original coordinate.

A piece may be rotated clockwise by 0,1,2 or 3 quarter-turns; reflection is forbidden. After one clockwise turn, [top,right,bottom,left] becomes [left,top,right,bottom]. Every outward-facing perimeter edge must be flat, and every edge facing another board cell must be nonflat and match its neighbor. Input is not guaranteed solvable.

Return exactly size*size pairs when solvable. pieceIndex is the zero-based row index in the supplied pieces, and each index occurs exactly once. The pair list is ordered by board rows from top left to bottom right; it is not the order of the input pieces. Return [] only for impossibility. Preserve all input rows and their order/values.

This callable makes the public Puzzle.solve/getCurrentSolution behavior executable with an explicit edge encoding and bounded board size. It does not ask for a UI, generation from hidden coordinates, or comparison with one preselected original assembly.
why: Fill the board in row-major order. At a new cell, its top and left neighbors are already fixed, so those two edge matches and the perimeter rules can be checked immediately. Try each unused piece in each of four rotations; undo a choice if its remaining suffix cannot be completed. Backtracking is necessary for a general feasibility contract: a locally fitting piece need not imply the rest of the puzzle is solvable.
correctness: Maintain a prefix containing distinct input pieces, with all perimeter edges and all already adjacent pairs valid. Each candidate checks all four perimeter requirements and the existing top/left joins, so appending it preserves the invariant. At a full board, every input piece occurs once and every join was checked when its later endpoint was placed, yielding a valid assembly. For completeness, consider any valid completion of the current prefix. The search enumerates its next unused piece and its rotation; those pass all local checks. Induction therefore reaches that completion unless an earlier valid solution was already returned. If every branch fails, no completion exists. Undoing the used flag restores the parent search state; the input pieces are never rotated in place.
walkthrough: For size 2 and pieces [[0,1,2,0],[0,0,3,-1],[-2,4,0,0],[-3,0,0,-4]], [0,0] fits top left. [1,0] fits top right because its left edge -1 matches 1 and its top/right edges are flat. [2,0] fits bottom left with top -2 matching 2. [3,0] closes the board: top -3 matches 3 and left -4 matches 4. Thus [[0,0],[1,0],[2,0],[3,0]] is valid. Rotating the entire completed board can yield another accepted answer. Replacing only edge -4 with -99 leaves unmatched identifiers and makes this board impossible.
time: For p=size^2 pieces, O(p*p!*4^p) is a conservative exhaustive-search upper bound, including candidate scans at partial boards. Early edge/perimeter pruning and unique matching identifiers make the supplied cases much smaller; no polynomial worst-case search claim is required.
space: O(p) auxiliary used flags, placements and recursion depth, excluding input and returned placement pairs. Each attempted orientation reads four edges without copying or mutating the input puzzle.
edges: A single all-flat piece versus a singleton with a nonflat perimeter edge.
Shuffled/rotated corners, edges and center; odd board side 3.
Unmatched or same-sign edges, unsolvable arrangements, and global rotations with multiple valid answers.
Returning duplicated piece indices, using reflections or changing the caller puzzle is invalid.
related: The primary Piece/Edge/Puzzle classes establish rotation, flat borders, complementary matching and assembly. The public greedy solver relies on its generated puzzle structure; this independently authored backtracking version also reports failure for the explicitly admitted unsolvable inputs.

languageWhy.csharp: C# local Edge/Search functions capture only owned placement/used arrays. Each output row is distinct; setting a used flag is undone after a failed recursive suffix. Arrays.Empty<int[]>() is the no-solution result.
languageWhy.java: Java uses a local Searcher class to recurse while capturing the final input references and owned arrays. The class reads pieces through edge(index,turn,side); it never rotates input rows. The returned int[][] has one independent pair row per position.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ const vector references prevent input mutation. std::function recursion captures owned placements and vector<bool> flags by reference. Modulo uses side-turn+4, which is nonnegative for the four allowed turns. The returned vector is an owned value.
languageWhy.python: Python uses a nested search with a used list and placement tuples. Modulo by four correctly maps a rotated side back to its original edge. The result converts tuples into concrete pair lists only after a complete successful search.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript closures retain only owned arrays; each successful tentative position receives a fresh [index,turn] pair. side-turn+4 avoids negative remainder. Recursion returns a boolean separately from the result array, so an impossible branch cannot be confused with a partially filled solution.

description: Implement the state transitions of a Minesweeper game: reveal a hidden cell, toggle a flag, expand connected blank areas, and stop after winning or hitting a bomb. The bomb layout is supplied explicitly so the exercise and tests are deterministic. Return a complete visible-board snapshot before play and after every requested action. Do not implement a bomb-location solver or reveal hidden bombs merely because the caller supplied the layout.
constraints: bombs is a rectangular 1..12 by 1..12 matrix of 0 (safe) and 1 (bomb), containing at least one safe cell. All cells initially are hidden and unflagged; the game is running. Every safe revealed cell displays the count of bombs in its eight surrounding positions, excluding itself and out-of-bounds positions.

actions has 0..100 rows [row,column,kind]. kind=0 requests reveal; kind=1 toggles a flag. Coordinates are signed 32-bit integers; out-of-bounds requests are rejected without changing state. A flag can be toggled only on a hidden or already flagged cell. Revealing a flagged or previously revealed cell is rejected; rejected requests have accepted=0.

Revealing a hidden safe zero exposes its eight-neighbor connected component of safe zero cells and the safe numbered boundary of that component. Flagged cells remain hidden and block expansion through that cell. They must be unflagged and revealed later if needed for winning. A numbered safe cell reveals only itself. A bomb reveal exposes that bomb and loses immediately. Flagging a bomb does not lose.

Win exactly when every safe cell is exposed; flags are not required on bombs. After a win or loss, all further requests are rejected without changing visible cells or outcome. A valid reveal/flag operation has accepted=1 even when it ends the game.

Return actions.length+1 integer rows. Each row is [state,accepted,...visibleCellsInRowMajorOrder], where state=0 running, 1 won, 2 lost. Initial accepted=0. Visible cell codes are 0..8 for an exposed safe count, 9 hidden, 10 flagged, 11 exposed bomb. Only the bomb actually hit is exposed on loss; other cells retain their prior display. Preserve the caller bomb/action matrices and rows.

This callable captures the public Board/Game reveal/flag/blank-expansion behavior using deterministic supplied layouts and machine-readable snapshots. Random board generation and console/UI parsing are outside the callable; no gameplay guessing is required.
why: Separate the immutable bomb layout from the player-visible board. A reveal changes each safe cell from hidden to exposed at most once, so marking it before putting a zero into the queue prevents repeated work and duplicate counters. Expanding only zeros includes their numbered boundary without propagating past numbered cells. Keep a remaining-safe count: reaching zero is precisely the winning condition, independent of flags on bombs.
correctness: Initially the visible board is all hidden and remainingSafe equals the number of safe cells. Reveal accepts only a hidden unflagged cell. If it is a bomb, exposing it and setting loss is correct. Otherwise exposing it computes the exact adjacent count and decrements remainingSafe once. A newly exposed zero is queued; its safe unflagged neighbors are exposed, and only new zeros are queued, so the queue reaches exactly the permitted zero-connected region and safe boundary. Already exposed or flagged cells are skipped, preventing double counting and flag changes during expansion. Thus remainingSafe always equals the unexposed safe-cell count; zero implies and is implied by victory. Flag operations change only hidden/flag state. Rejected and terminal operations change nothing. Each copied snapshot consequently records the exact resulting state without aliasing later updates.
walkthrough: For bombs [[0,1],[0,0]], reveal [1,0,0] exposes count 1, giving [0,1,9,9,1,9]. Flag [0,1,1] gives [0,1,9,10,1,9]. Revealing that flagged bomb [0,1,0] is rejected, giving [0,0,9,10,1,9]. Reveal the other safe cells [0,0,0] and [1,1,0]; the last snapshot is [1,1,1,10,1,1], a win. The flag is preserved and no bomb was exposed.
time: O(R*C + Q*R*C) time for R rows, C columns and Q actions, including the required full-board snapshots. Across the entire game each safe cell is exposed at most once and each zero scans at most eight neighbors; snapshot copying dominates long action sequences.
space: O(R*C) auxiliary visible board and zero-expansion queue, plus O((Q+1)*R*C) returned snapshot storage. The immutable input layout is not duplicated by the solver.
edges: No bombs, a single safe cell, eight-neighbor rather than four-neighbor counts.
Flag/unflag, flagged bomb reveal, flagged zero blocking expansion, repeated reveals.
Invalid coordinates, first-move loss, safe-only win and ignored requests after either terminal outcome.
Snapshots must retain prior contents instead of sharing one changing row.
related: The primary Java Board, Cell, UserPlay and Game classes establish flags, eight-neighbor blank expansion, safe-cell counting and terminal game state. This implementation fixes unintended flagged-bomb loss and makes rejection/terminal behavior explicit rather than copying source defects.

languageWhy.csharp: C# local Snapshot and Expose functions capture owned board/counter state. List<int[]> stores fresh snapshot arrays and queue coordinates. Marking a cell before queue insertion ensures a repeated neighbor scan never decrements remaining twice.
languageWhy.java: Java local Observer methods capture mutable one-element counter/state arrays and owned visible rows. The queue uses ArrayList with an advancing head rather than remove(0); every snapshot is a new int[] and toArray returns concrete rows.
languageWhy.cpp: C++ reads both input matrices through const references. Lambdas mutate only owned visible/trace vectors and scalar state. Queue coordinates are copied before possible vector growth, avoiding references invalidated by push_back.
languageWhy.python: Python nested helpers use nonlocal only for the remaining-safe counter. Each snapshot flattens current values into a fresh list. A list plus monotonically increasing head processes zeros without front-deletion shifts; visible marking prevents duplicate enqueue.
languageWhy.javascript: JavaScript closures maintain owned visible rows, counters and trace. Each snapshot builds a fresh flat array. The queue is traversed by index, and each exposed safe cell changes from code 9 before it can be enqueued again.
